title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a matching failure in an automated license plate reader. The Flock cameras read only letters and numbers and not plate backgrounds, so two plates carrying the same characters are the same string to the system. Kansas issues more than 100 plate designs, about half of them specialty, and duplicates numbers across them. The system was therefore operating outside the condition that makes plate matching meaningful, which is that a plate number identifies one vehicle.

The failure surfaced at the point where an alert reaches an officer in the field. In Colwich, Kansas, a camera alerted police and an officer recognized the Spurlocks' minivan and found the wrong plate type had been entered. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another alert led to a stop with guns drawn and handcuffs. A Wichita police captain said an alert alone is not enough for a stop, but that a wrong plate entry can leave officers no choice. Catching this before a stop would have required either plate numbers unique to a single vehicle, which Kansas is moving toward with seven digit non duplicated numbers, or a check that distinguishes plate type before the alert reaches an officer.

What is not established is fault or intent. The reporting comes from a single outlet's investigation, no finding has been made against Flock or any police agency, and the discussion of training the system to recognize plate backgrounds is described as a discussion, not a change.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were pulled over twice because their Kansas KU Alumni specialty plate, number 7007, matched a stolen GMC pickup's temporary tag. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police, but an officer recognized their minivan and found the wrong plate type had been entered. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock alert led police to stop them with guns drawn and handcuffs. Wichita police Capt. Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, so they cannot tell specialty plates apart. Kansas has more than 100 plate designs, about half specialty, and it duplicates numbers.

Slaughter said a Flock alert is not enough for a stop, but a wrong plate entry can leave officers no choice. He said such mistakes are rare, and Wichita police discussed training Flock's AI to recognize plate backgrounds. Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit, non duplicated numbers as the best solution. The Spurlocks' stolen vehicle entry has expired, so they no longer worry, and they plan to keep their 14 year old plate.
